A1-A2.headline: Walking and Cycling for Better Health

pages.text:
Walking to work or riding a bike uses only your own body to move. People also stay active when they run, row, or skate.

When towns build safe paths, many more people choose to ride bikes each day.
pages.caption: The urban bicycle, one of the most widespread and well-known vehicles for active mobility

pages.text:
Health tests show that daily walks and bike rides keep hearts strong. Moving each day helps people stay fit and avoid gaining too much weight. It fights the harm of sitting still for too many hours.

Being out on the street also lets people breathe fresh air, see their town, and greet neighbors on the way.

Taking a bike or walking instead of driving a car helps keep the air clean. Normal cars put tons of bad gas into the sky each year. That gas makes the Earth grow warm much faster.

When more people walk and ride, cities have cleaner air and far less traffic on busy roads near homes and shops.

Safe walks and bike lanes also help families save a lot of money. Cars cost a great deal to buy, fill with gas, and fix each year. Bikes cost much less, so almost anyone can own one.

With safe paths across town, more people can get to jobs, schools, parks, and health shops without a car.

In the United States, fewer people walk or ride bikes each day than in many like nations. One big reason is that wide roads often feel unsafe.

High death rates for walkers and bike riders keep careful people inside their cars. Now leaders are paying for safe lanes that link parks and city centers.

B1-B2.headline: Why Active Mobility Strengthens Cities and Health

pages.text:
Often called active travel, active mobility uses human effort to get around—from walking and cycling to running, rowing, and skating.

Smart city spending shows that safe paths can lift daily bike use sharply.
pages.caption: The urban bicycle, one of the most widespread and well-known vehicles for active mobility

pages.text:
Health studies clearly link regular active travel with healthier hearts and lower weight risks. Public health reports show that daily walking and cycling help counter the harm of sitting for long hours.

Moving outside also gives walkers and riders a richer feel for local streets and closer contact with neighbors.

Shifting short daily trips away from private cars brings fast gains for crowded towns. Regular family cars release tons of carbon gas every year, which speeds up global climate warming.

Growing active travel cuts dirty exhaust from city air while easing heavy traffic jams along busy neighborhood streets.

Spending on walkable streets and bike paths also brings fairer choices across city areas. Unlike cars that demand gas, repair bills, and upkeep, bikes stay within reach for nearly every household.

Safe, linked routes make it much easier for residents to reach jobs, schools, and local services each day.

Across the United States, active travel still lags behind peer nations, in part because many wide streets lack safe space for people outside cars.

High death rates among walkers and cyclists make cautious commuters stay in their cars. Now federal transport plans fund more protected paths linking parks and city districts.

C1-C2.headline: Active Mobility: Public Health, Equity, and Urban Design

pages.text:
Encompassing walking, urban cycling, running, and other non-motorized transit, active mobility harnesses human physical effort for daily travel.

Where cities build coherent bike networks, commuting participation rises steadily.
pages.caption: The urban bicycle, one of the most widespread and well-known vehicles for active mobility

pages.text:
Extensive health evidence demonstrates how active mobility counters sedentary mortality while simultaneously easing urban congestion. Clinical reports link daily walking and cycling to lower body mass indices and stronger cardiovascular resilience.

Beyond physical outcomes, unshielded outdoor transit cultivates sharper sensory awareness and civic connection.

Decarbonizing short-distance urban trips yields substantial environmental gains by displacing high-emission private automobiles. Because conventional passenger cars discharge large volumes of carbon dioxide annually, modal shifts help delay ecological tipping thresholds.

Quieter, cleaner corridors also restore everyday livability across dense neighborhoods.

Equally compelling, active mobility infrastructure strengthens economic equity across underserved metropolitan districts. Avoiding the steep purchase, fuel, and insurance costs of car ownership grants lower-income households dependable, affordable mobility.

Well-connected sidewalks and cycleways broaden access to education and gainful employment.

Within the United States, disproportionate pedestrian and cyclist fatalities have long discouraged widespread adoption of active mobility.

For decades, street designs prioritized rapid vehicle throughput over vulnerable road users at hazardous intersections. Federal transport initiatives now increasingly back protected lanes connecting communities safely.
